If these loads were flexible in similar levels to the loads analyzed in this study, the system peak reduction impacts (and results that are closely tied to peak reduction, such as effective shed) could be scaled up by 50% to get an approximation of the total potential flexibility on the grid. However, future work should include developing specific load dispatch algorithms and/or performance assumptions for these end uses to better understand their price response potential. The remaining 40% is from lighting, electronics, cooking, ventilation, and other loads that have limited or unknown pathways to load flexibility. Many of these end uses could be made “flexible” by adding storage within the devices (e.g. small battery packs in lighting fixtures), but the analysis of such potential is more akin to the BESS value proposition analysis than the actual flexing/shifting of end use loads. If it is thought that this sort of end-use-distributed storage may be lower cost than larger standalone battery systems, then they should certainly be analyzed as an alternative load flexing technology. While this study covers a significant portion of the load that occurs when the system is peaking, the balance across the entire year is quite different, as shown in the right panel of Figure 40. Of the 227 TWh of electricity demand modeled for 2030 (note that this includes all of the load in California’s IOU territories, not the entire state), only 42 TWh (18%) goes towards the end uses analyzed in this study. An additional 66 TWh (30%) is in the end uses described above as potentially flexible but not modeled in this study, while 118 TWh, or 52% of the electricity consumption in the state, is consumed by the unknown or unlikely to be flexible loads. As year- round load flexibility (i.e. beyond peak load reduction) becomes increasingly important, so will the need to identify and analyze pathways to make more of these loads flexible. 60 Figure 40. End use loads modeled in this study (colored), alongside out-of-scope loads that are likely flexible (e.g., refrigeration, commercial and medium-heavy duty EVs, and industrial processes) and unlikely to be flexible (e.g., lighting, electronics, cooking). 4.4.3 Enabling technologies The development of price responsive technologies is crucial for realizing the full potential of electricity load flexibility and hourly dynamic pricing. These technologies may exist for simple load scheduling or response to time-of-use price structures, but new capabilities must be developed to receive and respond to a price that varies every hour. A significant barrier to the development of such capabilities is the limited availability of actual dynamic tariffs for customers to go on. Manufacturers are hesitant to invest in developing capabilities that have no practical application in the current market. As we move closer to the required 2027 offerings of such tariffs, manufacturers and others who wish to provide automation services are expected to increasingly offer such capabilities. The availability of such tariffs will create a compelling market demand, driving innovation and reducing costs.
